subtype: Approach: switching from wandering to staying and asking [Revision]
passage: Paulo had already walked two lanes of the Sunday market in Singapore's Little India, and every stall looked the same: flowers, bangles, phone covers. His family was at none of them. Each corner took him farther from where they had started, and his throat felt tight. He stopped short. "I keep moving and they keep not being here." Beside a chai stall he planted his feet, took a breath and looked up at the owner, a woman named Ada. "Please, can you call my father? I'm lost." Ada wiped her hands and picked up her phone. Paulo sat on an upturned crate and watched the crowd, this time only waiting.

qa.q: Where did Paulo stop to ask for help?
qa.a: He stopped beside a chai stall.

qa.q: What was Paulo feeling when he stopped short?
qa.a: Paulo felt anxious, his throat tight, and he realised his walking was making things worse, since each corner took him farther from his family.

qa.q: What could Paulo have done from the start, and why?
qa.a: He could have stayed near the place he last saw his family and asked a stall owner for help, because his family would come back there.

qa.q: How might Ada see Paulo's request?
qa.a: She sees a boy who asks politely and clearly, so she can act at once by picking up her phone.

grounding: A boy who wanders and makes things worse switches to staying and asking a stall owner to phone his father.

subtype: Approach: switching from wandering to staying and asking [Revision]
passage: The weekly haat was held in the school grounds every Thursday, and it was packed. Shankar lost his father near the vegetable carts. He walked one lane looking for him, then another. More people. More stalls. No Papa. His legs were tired, and he felt more lost with every step. At the end of the second lane he stopped. "I'm moving, Papa's moving," he thought. "We'll never meet this way." There was a chai stall run by a man he recognised from the school canteen, Kamal bhaiya. Shankar went up to him. "Kamal bhaiya, I've lost my father. Can you phone him?" He gave the number. Kamal bhaiya dialled, then handed him a glass of water. "Sit here. Your papa's coming."

qa.q: Where did Shankar lose his father?
How did Shankar feel after walking two lanes without finding his father?
qa.a: He felt tired and more lost with every step, which made him stop and think.

qa.q: What else could Shankar have done even sooner, and why?
qa.a: He could have stopped straight away at a stall near the vegetable carts and asked for help, because staying put makes it easier to be found.

qa.q: How does the request look to Kamal bhaiya?
qa.a: Kamal bhaiya sees a boy he recognises asking calmly for help, so he is happy to phone and give him water while he waits.

grounding: It shows a boy realising that wandering makes being lost worse, stopping at a chai stall and asking the owner to phone his father.

subtype: Approach: switching from wandering to staying and asking [Revision]
passage: I help at my uncle's tea stall at the Sunday market, and I saw a boy, Harish, go past us three times in ten minutes. First walking fast, looking everywhere. Then slower, looking scared. The third time he stopped right in front of the stall and stood very still. Then he came up to my uncle and said, "Uncle, I've lost my father. I kept walking and it's getting worse. Can you call him?" He said the number carefully. My uncle called, and I gave Harish a stool. His father came in about five minutes, sweaty and relieved. I don't know what Harish was thinking when he stopped. But he looked calmer after he'd decided.

qa.q: How many times did Harish pass the tea stall?
What might Harish have been feeling on the third pass?
qa.a: He was probably scared and tired, though the helper at the stall can only guess from how he stood still.

qa.q: What else could Harish do next time he gets separated, and why?
qa.a: He could stop and ask a stall-keeper straight away, because each lane he walks makes it harder to be found.

qa.q: How does the day look to the helper at the tea stall?
qa.a: The helper notices a scared boy wandering and is glad to help by giving him a stool while the father is called.

grounding: It shows a boy switching from wandering to staying at a tea stall and asking the owner to phone his father.
